title: Rate limits, quotas, and reserved throughput

opening.headline: On days when traffic spikes, to prevent the service from failing due to 429 errors, distinguish between understanding the types of limits and methods for increasing them, as well as strategies to avoid them through design.
body: Normally, a service functions without issues, but on event days, it suddenly starts returning 429 errors. Service providers set usage limits, and if these limits are unknown during design, user requests during peak times will fail outright.

In this class, we first examine what rate limiting measures, how allocated capacity differs from system limits, and how to identify the causes when receiving a 429 response. We then review a pre-allocated throughput approach and practice by exploring how to combine limit escalation, design avoidance, and reservation in the context of traffic surges.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the concepts of rate limiting, allocation, and provisioned throughput.
You can distinguish between methods of increasing the limit and methods of avoiding it through design, and choose the appropriate combination.

paragraphs: A service that typically handles five requests per second experienced a significant increase in traffic, with 50 requests per second arriving on the event day. As a result, a substantial number of responses returned a 429 error. This indicates that the provider exceeded its request rate limit, not that the server failed.

The limit is not set by the user but imposed by the provider. Normally, the system operates below this limit and remains undetectable; however, at peak times, it suddenly becomes apparent. If the limit is not understood during design, user requests will fail directly during peak periods.

The approach can be broadly categorized into two methods: one involves increasing the limit itself, and the other involves designing systems to reduce usage and thereby avoid hitting the limit. These two methods differ in cost and performance, so they should be distinguished and applied appropriately. This course focuses on developing the judgment to differentiate between these methods and combine them effectively.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Will all 429 errors be resolved by simply waiting a moment and retrying? We verify how to explain the types of 429 responses during class.

screens.outro: First, let me recall whether I have ever experienced increasing the limit.

screens.title: Recall experience of requesting an increase in credit limit
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are presented. Since you're not entering or submitting an answer, take a moment to reflect on your own experience first.

items.prompt: Have you ever requested an increase in your credit limit? How long did it take?
items.answer: Upscaling does not typically happen immediately. In Claude documentation, organizations are automatically assigned to tiers based on their usage history and account status, and they may upgrade to higher tiers over time. OpenAI also automatically upgrades a user's tier when their accumulated credit purchase reaches a specified threshold. Expecting an upgrade request to be processed promptly in urgent situations may result in delays.

items.prompt: Is increasing the limit and using less the same solution?
items.answer: They are entirely different approaches. The first approach involves working with the provider to raise the ceiling limit itself, while the second approach involves reconfiguring your own design—such as relocating workloads, smoothing request flow through queuing, and reducing input tokens via caching. These two methods are often used together.

items.prompt: Have you ever checked your limit before encountering a failure due to limit constraints?
items.answer: Limits vary depending on the current state of the account, so they should be checked in advance. They can be viewed on the console's limits page, and Claude can read limits programmatically via the Rate Limits API. By periodically reading the limits rather than hardcoding them into the code, the values remain accurate even if they change.

screens.outro: We will check on a company-by-company basis what each one's limit is.

screens.title: Types of rate limits: RPM, TPM, RPD
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify how each company's limit is measured and what unit it is applied to.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: The Gemini API limits are measured across three axes: requests per minute (RPM), tokens per minute (TPM), and requests per day (RPD). Exceeding any one of these limits results in an error. For example, if the RPM limit is set to 20, an error occurs on the 21st request within any one minute—even if there is available headroom for token usage. These limits apply at the project level, not per API key, and daily limits are reset at midnight Pacific Time. Image generation models have additional separate limits, such as images per minute (IPM).

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI enforces limits based on RPM, RPD, TPM, TPD, images per minute (IPM), and other metrics. The first limit encountered is applied. Even if token limits remain available, requests will be blocked if the request volume limit is reached. These limits are organized at the organization and project level, not per user, and vary by model. Some model families share their limits, meaning that a single call consumes from the limit of other models within the same family.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude's Messages API limits are measured in requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM), and output tokens per minute (OTPM), and vary by model series. These limits apply at the organizational level and differ based on usage tier. Using a token bucket mechanism, the capacity is not reset at fixed intervals and continues to fill up until it reaches its maximum limit. In most models, input tokens read from cache are not counted toward ITPM, which effectively increases the limit due to caching.

tabs.label: Short interval surge
tabs.body: The limit can apply even within time intervals shorter than the specified unit time. The Claude document explains that a per-minute limit of 60 requests can be applied on a per-second basis at 1 request per second, meaning a burst of requests within a short time period could exceed the limit, even if the average per minute remains within the limit. This is why requests must be smoothly queued to avoid exceeding the limit.

data.notes: In Google Cloud's Agent Platform, limits are divided into allocated limits and system limits. Allocated limits have default values and are typically adjustable, while system limits are fixed and cannot be changed. Understanding this distinction allows you to request adjustable limits and avoid designing around immutable limits.

screens.outro: When hitting the limit and receiving error 429, I will confirm that the response varies depending on the cause.

screens.title: How to determine the cause when receiving error 429
screens.lead: When you select a response type, the cause and remedy are displayed. Review them in the order of the status code and error information.

items.answer: This means that in a short interval, rates such as RPM, ITPM, or OTPM have exceeded their rate limits. If you wait for the duration specified in the header and then retry, the request will be accepted. In this case, the design that adjusts request rates—specifically, the use of queues and backoff—is effective.

items.prompt: A 429 error with error_code enforced_spend_limit_reached without retry-after
items.answer: This indicates that the monthly expenditure limit has been reached. This is a rate_limit_error type similar to rate limit errors, but without a retry-after header; all retries, including those automatically handled by the SDK, continue to fail until access is restored. Either increase the limit or wait until the next month's initialization.

items.prompt: When the same input results in an HTTP 400 error and the specified usage limit message.
items.answer: I have reached the expenditure limit I set directly. The error type is invalid_request_error, and the message begins with "the API usage limit has been reached as specified. Access is restored when I increase or remove the limit I set.

It occurs when either RPM, TPM, or RPD exceeds a threshold, or when the 10-minute spend-based limit is exceeded. Depending on which limit is exceeded, a decision must be made regarding whether to wait, reduce the request size, or request an increase. The evaluation order is to first read the status code and error code, then determine whether to wait based on the presence of a retry-after header; if no retry-after is present, the process proceeds to increase the limit.

screens.outro: Let's examine methods for pre-allocating capacity instead of increasing limits.

screens.title: Provisioned Throughput and Capacity Reservation
screens.lead: When an item is selected, its description expands. Check in sequence whether the reservation method for throughput is appropriate and under what conditions.

items.title: Provisioned Throughput: Reserving throughput at a fixed cost
items.body: The Provisioned Throughput of the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is a subscription with a fixed cost and fixed duration, reserving a specified model's throughput at a chosen location. The duration can be selected from various options. To reserve, you must specify the model and the execution location.

items.title: When is it suitable to use?
items.body: The document outlines four conditions: when developing real-time operational services such as chatbots or agents, when the core workloads require consistently high throughput, when aiming to provide users with a consistent and predictable experience, and when seeking to predict costs with fixed pricing on a per-week or per-month basis while controlling overages.

items.title: Distinction between fixed-quantity and reservation methods
items.body: Google's throughput allocation documentation divides the methods for securing throughput into two categories: a pay-as-you-go model, where you pay only for what you use, and a reserved throughput model, where a fixed amount of throughput is pre-booked at a fixed price. Within the pay-as-you-go model, there are also standard, priority, and flex variants that allow you to balance cost and performance.

items.title: OpenAI Reserved Tier: Purchase capacity in dollars per minute
items.body: OpenAI Reserved Tier allows customers to pre-purchase throughput on a per-model basis in dollar amounts per minute, adding to their existing limits and enabling usage during periods of high demand. Usage exceeding the reserved amount will be charged at the standard volume rate. This tier is not available for batch or Flex usage.

items.title: Reservation risk: waste when baseline utilization is low
items.body: Reservation incurs costs even if not utilized. If normal usage is significantly lower than the reserved amount, that portion of fixed cost becomes wasted. Therefore, before making reservations, it is necessary to measure baseline usage, reserve only up to that baseline, and handle any usage exceeding the baseline on a pay-as-you-go basis.

screens.outro: Now let's combine these options to examine a case of sudden traffic surge.

screens.title: Explanation of conditions requiring reserved throughput under surge traffic scenarios
screens.lead: The instructor will sequentially walk through the methods for responding to event traffic. Select arrows to advance step by step and follow the decision process.

steps.title: Assumption
steps.body: Normally, 5 requests per second, and during events, up to 50 requests per second. The current limit is 20 requests per second. Some services are chatbots that customers wait for, while others allow for delays in classification tasks. These numbers are assumptions for illustrative purposes.

steps.title: Step 1. Peak factor calculation
steps.body: Dividing a peak of 50 items into a limit of 20 items results in a 2.5-fold increase. Under normal conditions, with a baseline of 5 items, there was previously a 4-fold buffer within the limit; however, during peak periods, the limit must exceed 2.5 times. This number determines the extent of required capacity. It is difficult to accommodate a gap exceeding 2.5 times through a single method.

steps.title: Step 2. Design to avoid the trap
steps.body: If work that allows for delays is removed from the queue, immediate calls decrease and a separate throttling budget can be utilized. By queuing requests and processing them at a rate below the limit, brief spikes in traffic can be smoothly absorbed. When receiving a 429 response, retry after the specified time and attempt again using exponential backoff. Using caching increases available headroom because input tokens read from cache are no longer consumed by ITPM.

steps.title: Step 3. Increase the limit
steps.body: Parts that cannot be avoided through design increase the limit. Users can accumulate usage history to enable automatic tier upgrades, request higher limits, or request quota adjustments. However, upward scaling may take time and is not guaranteed, and system limits may not change even when requested, so schedules must be planned with sufficient buffer.

steps.title: Step 4. Reservation Judgment
steps.body: If peaks are frequent and responses must be immediate, and if requests cannot be dropped, then review the reserved throughput. Conditions requiring consistently high throughput and predictable experiences—such as real-time chatbots—make reservation appropriate. If events occur only once or twice per year, reservation is wasteful and sufficient design and scaling will suffice.

steps.title: Step 5. Mix: allocate the baseline as reserved, excess as limited quantity
steps.body: Actual design is typically a combination. Normal baseline usage is reserved in advance, while peak usage above the baseline is handled on a volume basis, smoothed out using queues and scheduling. The limits are not fixed in code but are periodically read, ensuring the design remains consistent even if limits change.

screens.outro: Summarize the key points at the final screen.

screens.title: The limit is an input value for capacity planning.
screens.lead: This lesson's key points are summarized. Please review your answers to the questions posed in the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: Capacity is not a bottleneck but an input value used to plan throughput. First, determine whether RPM, TPM, or RPD is the bottleneck, as allocation can be requested for adjustment; however, system capacity remains fixed. Reserved throughput is acquired as a fixed cost to ensure consistent capacity.

Going back to the initial question, not all 429 errors are resolved by simply waiting. If a retry-after header is present, wait for that duration; however, when there's no retry-after header and the error_code indicates a rate limit, the limit must be increased. The response should combine both approaches—increasing the limit and designing to avoid the issue—by first calculating the peak multiplier to determine how large a response is required.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The requested quota and limit in the document are assumed for illustrative purposes. Directly verify the peak and current limits of my service and calculate accordingly.

checks.intro: Recall the type of 429 response you just saw and verify it for yourself. Results are not recorded.
checks.q:
A service received the following response. What is the most appropriate action?  
HTTP 429, rate_limit_error, details.error_code = "enforced_spend_limit_reached", no "retry-after" header
options: Since there is no header, immediately increase the retry count without performing a backoff.
Since the spending limit has been reached, further attempts are futile; instead, wait for the limit to be increased or access to be restored.
Since the requested rate exceeds the per-minute limit, slowly releasing the request through a queue resolves the issue immediately.
Due to a temporary server outage, sending the same request to a different model will resolve it.
checks.explain: This error_code indicates that the monthly spending cap has been reached, not a rate limit. It does not include a retry-after header, and retries—including SDK automatic retries—will fail until access is restored. The party responsible for increasing the cap must handle this.

wrong.0: Increasing the number of retry attempts continues to fail if the upper limit is not lifted.
wrong.2: Regulating request speed is a response to rate limits such as RPM, and this code represents an expenditure cap.
wrong.3: This is not a server failure issue but rather a problem with the organization's expenditure cap, and changing the model will not alter this cap.

checks.intro: Now recall the response sequence just explained and arrange it appropriately. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: When normal service volume is 5 requests per second, review the processing order when event volume reaches 50 requests per second (with a limit of 20 requests per second).
items: Calculate how many times the peak exceeds the limit.
Avoids designs such as extracting via batch, flowing through queues, and exponential backoff retry.
Increases the limit through tier scaling or allocation adjustment
If peaks are frequent and immediate response is required, review the reserved processing capacity.
checks.explain: Understand the scale first, design around it initially, then increase the limit; if still insufficient, review the reserved throughput.

glossary.def: Rate limits based on request volume or token count per unit time. Exceeding these limits results in a 429 error.
This is the upper limit of resource usage assigned to a project or organization, typically the value at which adjustments can be requested.
A subscription that reserves processing capacity for a specific model at a fixed cost and for a fixed period.
A system that determines whether to secure throughput using fixed allocation or reserved capacity.

The header attached to a 429 response indicates that the request should be retried after a few seconds. A 429 response lacking this header might indicate a hard limit that will not be resolved by waiting.

misconceptions.fact: This is mostly a signal that I have exceeded my limit. It is different from provider outages, and the response varies depending on the cause.

misconceptions.myth: The limit can be increased without any conditions.
misconceptions.fact: Upticks are slow and not guaranteed, and system limits cannot be changed. You must use methods to work around these limitations through design.
Low baseline usage results in wasted fixed costs. It is suitable for services that require continuous high throughput and predictability.
429 has reached the monthly expenditure limit and continues to fail even with retries, as it lacks a retry-after header. The limit must be increased based on the error code.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The limit is an input value of the capacity plan and the first encountered limit applies.
We distinguish and mention both limit increases and design avoidance together.
Reservation throughput is appropriate when continuous high throughput and predictability are required.
429 first checks whether to increase the limit for waiting based on retry-after and error_code.
